title: Design: URL shortener
objective: Design a URL shortener end to end: requirements, a rough estimate, the API, short codes, storage, caching and redirects.

sources.title: IETF RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), sections 15.4.2 and 15.4.3: 301 is heuristically cacheable; 302 Found is temporary

simplifies: One region and one database. All numbers are illustrative. Real services also need abuse checks on submitted URLs, custom aliases, link expiry, analytics pipelines and replication across regions.

steps.caption: Requirements: turn a long URL into a short code; visiting the short link redirects. Links are created rarely and visited often: reads far outnumber writes.
Estimate (illustrative): 10 million new links a month × about 500 bytes each ≈ 5 GB a month. Storage is easy; the real work is fast redirects.
API: POST /links with the long URL returns a code; GET /{code} answers with a redirect to the long URL.
Short codes: take the next number from a counter and write it in base 62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z). Seven characters give 62⁷, about 3.5 trillion codes, with no collisions to check.

predict.prompt: How many different 7-character codes can base 62 make?

options.explanation: Right. 62 choices for each of 7 places: 62 × 62 × … seven times.
That adds the places instead of multiplying the choices.
That is far too few; it would run out within a few months at our estimate.

steps.caption: Storage: a lookup by code is the only hot query, so a key-value table (code → long URL, keyed on code) fits.
Caching: popular links are visited constantly, so keep them in a cache. Most redirects never touch the database.

predict.prompt: Reads far outnumber writes, and a few links are very popular. Where should most redirects be answered?

options.text: From a cache in front of the database
options.explanation: Right. Hot links stay in the cache, so the database sees few reads.
It works, but every visit pays for a database read.
Browsers may cache some redirects, but the service still has to answer first visits.

steps.caption: Redirect status: 301 means moved permanently, and HTTP allows caching it, so later visits may skip your service. 302 is temporary, so visits come back through you and can be counted.

predict.prompt: You want to count every click. Which redirect should the service send?

options.explanation: Right. Visits keep coming back through the service, where they can be counted.
A 301 can be cached, so repeat visits may never reach your service to be counted.

options.text: 200 OK with the long URL in the page
options.explanation: That shows a page instead of redirecting.

steps.caption: Failure modes: if the database is down, the cache still answers hot links; rate-limit link creation so spammers can't flood the service.

quiz.prompt: Why use a counter (in base 62) rather than random codes?

options.text: Every code is unique, so there is nothing to check for collisions
options.explanation: Right. The trade-off: sequential codes are guessable, which matters if links should be private.

options.text: Counters make codes shorter than any other method
options.explanation: Length depends on how many codes you need, not the method.
They can; they just need a collision check.

quiz.prompt: The service is slow, and 95% of traffic is redirects for 1% of links. Best first step?

options.explanation: Right. That answers most traffic without touching the database.
Possible, but caching attacks the actual pattern more cheaply.
Code length doesn't affect redirect speed.
